claims.text: WTaTiVZr is equimolar, with approximately 20 at.% of each constituent.
The initial WTaTiVZr alloy is homogeneous and single-phase BCC.
Equimolar WTaTiVZr exhibits significant local lattice distortion.
Random atomic-size and bonding variations in WTaTiVZr generate local lattice distortions.
BCC tungsten has narrow screw-dislocation cores with high Peierls barriers.
Lattice distortions in WTaTiVZr broaden or destabilize screw-dislocation cores.
Core modification caused by compositional randomness diminishes the dominance of screw-dislocation-mediated plasticity.
Lattice distortion promotes activation and glide of <111>{110} edge dislocations in WTaTiVZr.
The proposed edge dislocations are less temperature-sensitive than the screw dislocations dominant in pure tungsten.
The proposed edge dislocations glide and multiply more readily at high temperature.
The shift from screw- to edge-dominated motion reduces the effective Peierls barrier for dislocation motion.
More readily mobile edge dislocations improve strain accommodation and deformation-energy dissipation.
At 800–900 °C, WTaTiVZr will have greater plastic strain and toughness than pure tungsten.
At 800–900 °C, WTaTiVZr will have lower apparent yield strength than pure tungsten.
Deformed WTaTiVZr will contain a higher proportion of mobile edge dislocations than deformed pure tungsten.
Pure tungsten has limited high-temperature plastic deformation and poor toughness because its plasticity relies on high-barrier screw dislocations.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply only while equimolar WTaTiVZr remains a homogeneous BCC alloy at approximately 800–900 °C.
Secondary phases or significant precipitates may cause deviations from the proposed dislocation mechanism.
The magnitude of the plastic-strain and toughness improvement depends on processing history and microstructural uniformity.
The effects of irradiation and plasma-related surface phenomena on the proposed behavior remain unquantified.
